This was indeed difficult!
He broadly sought wise men,
to assist your later heirs.
He established official punishments,
to warn those in positions.
Saying:
'Dare to have constant dancing in the palace,
and revelrous singing in the chambers,
this is called the shamanistic wind.'
Dare to be addicted to goods and sex,
constant in wandering and hunting,
this is called the dissolute wind.
Dare to insult the words of the sages,
reject loyalty and uprightness,
keep distant from the virtuous aged,
and associate with obstinate youths,
this is called the chaotic wind.
Of these three winds and ten offenses,
if a minister or officer has one upon his person,
his family will surely be lost;
if a ruler of a state has one upon his person,
his state will surely perish.
If subordinates do not correct him,
their punishment is tattooing.
Instruct this fully even to the lowest officers.
Alas!
The succeeding king should reverence his person.
Think upon this!
'The sages' plans are vast,
their good words are very clear.
Only God is not constant;
if you do good, he sends down all blessings;
if you do not good, he sends down all calamities.'
For your virtue, no act is too small—
the myriad states will celebrate;
for your lack of virtue, no act is too great—
you will overthrow your lineage."
After Tài Jiǎ was enthroned,
he was unenlightened,
so Yī Yǐn exiled him to Tóng,
and after three years he returned to Bó
and reflected on the constant way.
Yī Yǐn composed the three chapters of "Tài Jiǎ."
The successor king was not kind to the Grand Guardian,
so Yī Yǐn wrote a document saying:
The former king "beheld the bright mandate of Heaven,"
and thereby served the spirits above and below,
the altars of land and grain, and the ancestral temple
with all reverence and solemnity.
Heaven observed his virtue,
and thus bestowed the great mandate,
to pacify all regions.
I myself was able to assist my sovereign
in settling the multitudes,
thus the successor king greatly inherited the foundation and legacy.
"I myself first witnessed in the western city of Xià,
that when a ruler had constancy,
his ministers also had constancy."
Their later kings failed to have constancy,
and their ministers also lacked constancy.
Successor king, take warning!
Revere your sovereign duty,
"If the sovereign is not sovereign-like,
he shames his ancestors."
The king, however, paid no heed.
Yī Yǐn then said:
The former king, before dawn, would rise to brilliance,
sitting and waiting for daybreak,
widely seeking talented men,
"to enlighten and guide later generations."
"Do not overthrow your own mandate and ruin yourself,"
be cautious in your frugal virtue,
and think of long-term plans.
"Like drawing the bow on a catapult,
go and examine the notch against the measure, then release."
Revere your aims,
and follow the ways of your ancestors.
Thus I am pleased,
and for ten thousand generations there will be praise.
The king was unable to change.
Yī Yǐn said:
This is unrighteousness,
habits becoming nature.
"I cannot associate with the disobedient,"
so he built the Tóng Palace,
close to the former king, to instruct him,
that he might not be forever deluded.
The king went to dwell in mourning at Tóng Palace,
and was able to perfect his sincere virtue.
In the third year, on the first day of the twelfth month,
Yī Yǐn, with royal robes, welcomed the successor king back to Bó.
He composed a document saying:
"Without a sovereign,
the people cannot support each other to live;
without the people,
the sovereign has none to rule over the four quarters."
August Heaven favored and protected the Shāng,
enabling the successor king to perfect his virtue,
truly an endless blessing for ten thousand generations.
The king bowed and touched his head to the ground, saying:
I, the little one, was not clear about virtue,
making myself unworthy.
"Desires ruin measures,
indulgence ruins rites."
Thus I quickly brought blame upon myself.
"Heaven-sent calamities can still be avoided;
self-made calamities cannot be escaped."
Having previously turned away from the instructions of my mentor,
I failed at the beginning;
I still rely on your virtue of correction and rescue,
to plan for a good end.
Yī Yǐn bowed and touched his head to the ground, saying:
Cultivate your person,
make your sincere virtue harmonize with those below,
and you will be an enlightened sovereign.
The former king cherished the distressed and poor,
the people obeyed his commands,
none were displeased.
He united with the rulers of states. His neighbors
would say:
"We wait for our sovereign;
when our sovereign comes, there will be no punishments."
O king, strengthen your virtue,
look to your ancestors,
do not be idle or negligent at any time.
Serve your ancestors with filial piety,
receive subordinates with respect;
see far with clarity,
listen to virtue with acuity.
I will uphold the king's blessings without weariness.
Yī Yǐn further admonished the king, saying:
Alas!
Heaven has no constant affections,
it favors only those who are reverent.
The people do not constantly cherish,
they cherish only the benevolent.
Spirits and gods do not constantly enjoy sacrifices,
they enjoy only those from the sincere.
The position of Heaven is difficult!
With virtue, there is order;
without virtue, chaos.
Follow the same path as order,
and there is no lack of prosperity;
share the same actions as chaos,
and there is no lack of ruin.
From beginning to end, be careful in your associations,
and you will be a truly enlightened sovereign.
The former king thus diligently revered his virtue,
and was able to match God.
Now the king succeeds to a glorious heritage,
look to this as your mirror!
"If you ascend a height,
you must start from below;
if you travel far,
you must start from near."
Do not take the people's affairs lightly,
but regard them as difficult;
do not consider your position secure,
but regard it as perilous.
Be cautious of the end from the beginning.
If words go against your heart,
seek the principle in them;
if words accord with your will,
seek what is unprincipled in them.
Alas!
Without thought, how can you gain?
Without action, how can you achieve?
"When the one man is greatly good,
all states are thereby rectified."
Let the ruler not disrupt old governance with clever speech,
let ministers not dwell on success due to favor and profit;
then the state will long be maintained in excellence.
Yī Yǐn composed "All Have the One Virtue."
After Yī Yǐn had returned the government to his sovereign,
and was about to announce his return,
he set forth admonitions on virtue.
Saying:
Alas!
"Heaven is hard to rely on,"
"the mandate is not constant."
Make your virtue constant,
and preserve your position;
if your virtue is inconstant,
"the nine regions will be lost."
The Xià king could not use virtue,
disrespected spirits and oppressed the people;
August Heaven did not protect him,
looking over all regions,
enlightening and guiding those with the mandate,
seeking one with unified virtue,
to make him master of the spirits.
"I myself and Tāng,
both had the one virtue."
We were able to satisfy Heaven's heart;
received Heaven's bright mandate,
to lead the hosts of the nine regions,
and thus reform the Xià calendar.
It was not that Heaven favored us, the Shāng,
but that Heaven assists the one with unified virtue;
it was not that the Shāng sought the lower people,
but that the people turn to the one with unified virtue.
When virtue is unified,
no action is not auspicious;
when virtue is divided,
no action is not inauspicious.
Good and ill fortune do not err—it depends on the person;
Heaven sends down disaster or blessing—it depends on virtue.
Now the successor king newly undertakes his mandate,
renew your virtue,
from beginning to end be unified,
and this will be daily renewal.
Appoint officials based on worthiness and talent,
choose assistants based on their character.
Ministers serve the ruler to promote virtue,
serve below to benefit the people.
It is difficult and requires caution,
only harmony and unity.
Virtue has no constant teacher,
hold to goodness as your teacher;
goodness has no constant master,
unite in the ability to be one.
Make the myriad clans all say:
How great are the king's words!
And also say:
How unified is the king's heart!
Thus secure the blessings of the former kings,
and eternally ensure the livelihood of the masses.
Alas!
"From the temple of seven generations,
one can observe virtue;
from the leader of ten thousand men,
one can observe governance."
Without the people, the sovereign has none to command;
without the sovereign, the people have none to serve.
Do not exalt yourself and belittle others;
if even a single man or woman
fails to give their utmost,
the ruler of the people will have none to accomplish his tasks.
After Wò Dīng had buried
Yī Yǐn at Bó,
Jiù Dān then recorded the deeds of Yī Yǐn,
composing the "Wò Dīng".
The chapter is lost.
Yī Zhì served as minister to Tài Wù,
and in Bó, an ominous mulberry and grain grew together in the court.
Yī Zhì praised Wū Xián,
composing the four chapters of "Xián Yì".
The chapters are lost.
Tài Wù praised Yī Zhì,
composing the "Yī Zhì"
and "Yuán Mìng".
The chapters are lost.
Zhòng Dīng moved to Xiāo,
composing the "Zhòng Dīng".
The chapter is lost.
Hé Dǎn Jiǎ resided at Xiàng,
composing the "Hé Dǎn Jiǎ".
The chapter is lost.
Zǔ
Yǐ's capital at Gěng was destroyed,
and he composed the "Zǔ Yǐ".
The chapter is lost.
Pán Gēng moved the capital five times,
intending to establish it at Bó Yīn,
but the people lamented and complained.
Thus, the three chapters of "Pán Gēng" were composed.
When Pán Gēng moved to Yīn,
the people were not content with their new dwellings,
so he called upon the multitude
of concerned officials to express their views.
They said:
"Our king has come
and settled here;
he values our people,
not wishing to see them all perish.
If we cannot help each other to survive,
what use is divination?
Our former kings had their duties,
reverently obeying the Mandate of Heaven;
thus, they did not always remain in peace,
nor did they always stay in one city,
having moved to five capitals up to now.
If we do not follow the ancients,
how can we know Heaven's decisive mandate,
let alone continue the achievements of the former kings?
Like a fallen tree
that sprouts anew,
may Heaven grant us eternal life in this new city,
to restore the great enterprise of the former kings
and bring peace to the four quarters."
Pán Gēng educated the people,
relying on those in positions of authority,
to uphold the old practices and rectify the laws.
He said:
"Let no one dare to suppress
the admonitions of the common people!"
The king ordered the multitude to all come to the court.
The king spoke thus:
"Come, all of you.
I shall instruct you.
Set aside your selfish intentions,
and do not be arrogant or pursue comfort.
In ancient times, our former kings
also sought to employ seasoned officials in governance.
When the king announced his decrees,
they did not conceal his intentions,
and the king greatly respected them.
There were no irresponsible words,
and the people were greatly transformed.
Now you are clamorous,
spreading dangerous and superficial talk,
I do not know what you are disputing!
It is not that I have abandoned this virtue,
but that you conceal virtue, showing no fear
of me alone.
I see things as clearly as fire.
I too may lack clever strategies,
leading to your laxity.
Like a net attached to its main rope,
it is orderly and not tangled;
like farmers tilling the land and laboring diligently,
they will have a harvest in autumn.
If you can set aside your selfish hearts,
and bestow true virtue upon the people,
even reaching your relatives and friends;
then you may boldly declare,
'You have accumulated virtue!'
But if you do not fear the great harm near and far,
like lazy farmers content with ease,
not diligently laboring,
not tilling the fields,
then you will have no millet or grain.
If you do not spread good words among the people,
you will bring poison upon yourselves.
Then, with your wickedness and villainy,
you will bring disaster upon yourselves.
Since you first spread evil among the people,
you will bear the suffering,
and what use will regret be then?!
(Observe the petty people)
Observe the petty people,
they still heed admonitions.
If even they let slip careless words,
how much more can I control your lives and deaths!
Why do you not inform me
but instead stir each other with rumors?
The fear of sinking among the multitude,
the ease with which evil spreads like a fire
raging across the plains,
making it impossible to approach,
how can it be extinguished?
This is because you yourselves have created unrest,
it is not my fault!
Chí Rén once said:
'For people, we seek the old;
for vessels, we do not seek the old, but the new.'
In ancient times, our former kings,
along with your fathers and grandfathers,
shared both toil and ease;
how dare I impose unjust punishments?
For generations, your merits have been recognized,
and I will not conceal your goodness.
Now, as I make a great offering to the former kings,
your ancestors will also partake in the sacrifice.
Whether blessings or disasters come,
I too dare not employ undeserved virtue.
I warn you of the difficulties,
like an archer having a target.
Do not scorn the elderly or bully the adults,
do not neglect the young or despise the orphans.
Each of you, settle in your dwellings,
strive to exert your strength,
and follow my plans and commands.
Regardless of distance or proximity,
offenses will be punished with death,
while virtue will be rewarded to highlight goodness.
If the state prospers,
it is due to all of you;
if the state does not prosper,
it is I alone who bears the blame of neglect.
All of you, take this message to heart:
from now into the future,
each of you attend diligently to your duties,
fulfill your positions properly,
and guard your words.
If punishment reaches you, do not regret it."
Pán Gēng, intending to cross the river,
led the people in the migration.
He then addressed those who did not comply,
sincerely admonishing the multitude with honesty.
All gathered
hastily in the royal court,
and Pán Gēng ascended to address his people.
He said:
"Listen carefully to my words,
do not neglect or disobey my command.
Alas! In ancient times, our former rulers
always upheld the people's welfare.
The rulers and people shared concerns,
and rarely did they not align with the timing of Heaven.
When Yīn faced great calamity,
the former kings did not cling to the past; their actions
were guided by the benefit of the people in moving.
Why do you not consider the accounts of our ancient rulers?
I support and assist you,
desiring only shared peace and prosperity;
it is not that you are at fault,
subject to punishment.
I call upon you to cherish this new city,
also for your sake,
to greatly follow this intention.
Now I shall lead you in the migration,
to stabilize this state.
You do not worry about the troubles in my heart,
instead, you all greatly fail to reveal your hearts,
respectfully thinking with sincerity; moving me, the one alone.
You only bring upon yourselves exhaustion and hardship;
like riding in a boat,
if you do not cross,
the cargo will rot.
Your sincerity does not connect,
and you will only sink together.
If you do not examine this,
what good is anger to cure it?
You do not plan for the long term
to consider your calamities;
you greatly encourage worry.
Now you have the present but no future,
how will you survive under Heaven?"
Now I command you to be of one mind;
do not stir up filth
to make yourselves foul,
lest others corrupt your persons
and lead your hearts astray.
I appeal to Heaven to continue your lives;
how could I intimidate you?
It is to support and nurture you all.
I consider the toil of my divine ancestors for your forefathers;
I greatly wish to provide for you,
thereby cherishing you.
If I fail in governance,
lingering here,
my exalted ancestors will then severely
send down punishment and sickness,
saying:
"Why do you oppress my people?"
If you, the myriad people, do not strive to live,
nor share plans with me as one;
my ancestors will then send down upon you punishment and sickness,
saying:
"Why do you not unite with my young grandson?"
Thus, if there is any deviation in virtue,
from above they will punish you,
and you will have no escape.
In ancient times, my ancestors
toiled for your grandfathers and fathers,
and you are all my nurtured people.
If you harbor harm in your hearts,
my ancestors will inform your grandfathers and fathers;
your grandfathers and fathers
will then abandon you utterly,
and not save you from death.
Here, I have officials in government who disrupt order,
hoarding their shells and jades;
your ancestors and fathers
will then report to my exalted ancestors, saying:
"Inflict great punishment upon our descendants!"
Then my exalted ancestors will severely
send down misfortune.
Alas! Now I tell you: my decision is unchangeable.
Always revere this great concern,
do not distance yourselves from me;
you should share plans and thoughts to follow me,
each establishing fairness in your hearts.
If there are those who are inauspicious and unrighteous,
rebellious and disrespectful,
deceitful and treacherous;
I will cut off and exterminate them,
leaving no offspring,
not allowing them to propagate in this new city!
Go forth, and strive to live!
Now I shall lead you in moving,
to establish your homes forever."
After Pángēng had moved,
he settled their dwellings.
Then he rectified their positions,
and comforted the multitude.
He said:
"Do not be playful or idle; diligently establish
the great mandate.
Now I shall lay bare my heart and innermost thoughts,
and fully declare my intentions to all of you.
I do not blame you all,
and you should not collectively resent me,
nor join in slandering me.
In ancient times, my former kings sought to surpass previous achievements,
moving to the mountains;
thus they reduced our misfortunes,
and accomplished fine deeds for our state.
Now our people are scattered and displaced,
with no stable abode.
You ask me,
'Why disturb the myriad people to move?'
It is because God is about to restore the virtue of our great ancestor,
and bring order to our house.
I, being sincere and reverent,
respectfully undertake the people's mandate,
to settle forever in the new city.
Thus I, a young man,
do not disregard your counsel,
but each follows the divine guidance. I dare not oppose the divination,
but magnify this great undertaking.
Alas! Chiefs of states, heads of departments,
and all officers in charge of affairs,
may you all reflect deeply!
I will diligently observe you,
considering respect for my people.
I will not employ those fond of goods;
but dare to honor those who nurture life,
who support others and plan for their secure dwelling,
and shall order and esteem them.
Now that I have fully declared my intentions to you,
whether you agree or not, there must be no disrespect.
Do not hoard treasures and valuables,
but strive to live through your own efforts.
Spread virtue among the people,
and always be of one mind."
Gāozōng dreamed of obtaining Yuè,
and sent various artisans to seek him in the wilderness,
finding him at Fùyán.
He composed the three chapters of "The Charge to Yuè."
The king was in mourning,
observing the silence for three years.
After the mourning period ended,
he still did not speak.
All the ministers admonished the king, saying:
"Alas!
To know is called wisdom,
and wisdom truly sets an example.
The Son of Heaven rules over all states,
and all officials follow his model.
The king's words create commands;
if he does not speak, his ministers have nothing to receive as orders."
The king then made a writing to announce:
"With me as the standard for the four quarters,
I fear my virtue may not be adequate,
hence I do not speak."
He reverently remained silent, pondering the Way.
He dreamed that God bestowed upon him a good assistant,
to speak on his behalf.
Then he examined the image,
and had it used to search throughout the land.
Yuè was building walls in the wilderness of Fùyán,
and resembled the image;
thus he was set up as prime minister,
and the king placed him by his side.
He commanded him, saying:
"Morning and evening, impart teachings,
to assist my virtue.
Like metal,
I use you as a whetstone;
like crossing a great river,
I use you as a boat and oar;
like in a year of great drought,
I use you as a soaking rain.
Open your heart,
and irrigate my heart.
If medicine does not cause dizziness,
the illness will not be cured;
if walking barefoot, one does not look at the ground,
the feet will be injured."
You and your colleagues,
must be of one mind,
to correct your sovereign.
Lead in following the former kings,
guide me, the descendant of high ancestors,
to comfort the myriad people.
Alas!
Reverently follow my timely commands,
and you shall have a good end."
Yuè replied to the king, saying:
"Wood follows the plumb line and becomes straight;
the sovereign follows admonishment and becomes sage."
If the sovereign can be sage,
ministers will not need orders to obey;
who would dare not reverently follow the king's excellent commands?
When Yuè took charge of all officials,
he advanced and said to the king:
"Alas!
The enlightened king follows the Way of Heaven,
establishes states and sets up capitals,
appoints sovereigns and lords,
and supports them with ministers and heads,
not for ease and pleasure,
but to govern the people."
Heaven is all-seeing and all-hearing,
the sage king takes this as his model,
the ministers reverently follow,
and the people are governed and obedient.
"The mouth can bring shame,
armor and helmet can provoke war,
robes and garments are stored in chests,
shields and spears are used only after self-reflection."
If the king guards against these,
and truly can be discerning in them,
then nothing will not be excellent.
Order or disorder lies in the various officials;
appointments should not go to personal favorites,
but only to the capable.
"Rank should not be given to those of bad virtue,"
but only to the worthy.
Consider what is good before acting,
and act only when the time is right.
To boast of one's goodness,
is to lose that goodness;
to pride oneself on one's ability,
is to lose that merit.
Only when every affair is prepared,
with preparation there is no calamity.
Do not invite favor that brings insult,
nor be ashamed of faults and commit wrongs.
Only in their proper dwelling,
governance becomes pure.
"To be excessive in sacrifices,
is called irreverence.
Rites too numerous lead to chaos,
making it difficult to serve the spirits."
The king said:
"Excellent words!
Yuè! 'Your words should be followed,'
but if you do not speak well,
I will not hear of your actions."
Yuè bowed and touched his head to the ground,
saying:
"It is not knowing that is difficult,
but acting that is truly hard.
If the king is sincere, it is not difficult,
truly matching the accomplished virtue of the former kings.
If Yuè does not speak,
he will bear the blame."
The king said:
"Come, you, Yuè!
I, the young one, formerly studied with Gānpán,
then withdrew to the wilds,
entered and dwelt by the river,
and from the river went to Bó.
Until the end, there was no enlightenment.
You must instruct my will,
like making sweet wine,
you are the yeast;
'like preparing a harmonious soup,
you are the salt and plum.'
'You correct and improve me,
do not abandon me.'
I will be able to follow your teachings."
Yuè said:
"O king!
One seeks broad knowledge,
to establish affairs in time.
Learning from ancient teachings brings gain.
Affairs not modeled on antiquity
yet able to last forever—
such I have never heard.
'In learning,
humble your will, strive to be timely and diligent,
then cultivation will come.'
Truly cherish this,
and the Way accumulates in your person.
Remember
'teaching is half of learning,'
'think constantly of learning from start to end,'
and virtue will be cultivated unconsciously.
Look to the established laws of the former kings,
and you will never err.
I, Yuè, will respectfully uphold this,
broadly summoning the talented and virtuous,
to place them in various positions."
The king said:
"Alas!
Yuè!
Within the four seas,
all look up to my virtue—
this is your influence.
As limbs make a man,
good ministers make a sage.
Formerly, the ancient minister Bǎohéng assisted our former king,
and said:
'If I cannot make my sovereign like Yáo and Shùn,
my heart feels shame,
as if whipped in the marketplace.
If one man does not find his place,
I say it is my fault.'
He aided our illustrious ancestors,
reaching up to the great heaven.
You should brightly support me,
not let Āhéng alone have the glory of the Shāng.
Without worthies, the sovereign cannot govern;
without a sovereign, worthies cannot be sustained.
May you be able to assist your ruler like the former kings,
eternally comforting the people."
Yuè bowed and touched his head to the ground, saying:
"I dare to respond and extol the glorious mandate of the Son of Heaven."
When Gāozōng sacrificed to Chéngtāng,
a flying pheasant perched on the tripod's ear and crowed,
and Zǔjǐ admonished the king.
Thus were written "Gāozōng's Róng Sacrifice Day" and "The Admonitions of Gāozōng."
On Gāozōng's Róng sacrifice day,
there was a crowing pheasant.
Zǔjǐ said:
"First, rectify the king,
then set his affairs in order."
He then instructed the king, saying:
"Heaven oversees the people below,
governing with righteousness.
It grants years long and short;
it is not Heaven that cuts lives short,
but people who cut them off midway.
When people do not follow virtue,
and do not heed their crimes,
Heaven has already bestowed the mandate
to correct their virtue,
yet they say:
'What can it do to me?'
Alas! The king's heir must reverence the people.
All are Heaven's descendants;
in sacrifices, do not enrich [the rites] for the intimate."
When Yīn began to resent Zhōu,
and the Zhōu people attacked Lí,
Zǔyī grew fearful,
and rushed to report to Shòu.
Thus was written "The Western Lord Conquers Lí."
After the Western Lord had conquered Lí,
Zǔyī grew fearful,
and rushed to report to the king.
He said:
"Son of Heaven, Heaven is ending our Yīn mandate.
The wise men and great tortoise dare not see good fortune.
It is not that the former kings do not aid their descendants,
but the king, through excess and cruelty, has cut himself off.
Thus Heaven abandons us,
and we have no peace or food.
Not considering Heaven's nature,
not following the constant laws.
Now our people all wish us to perish,
saying: 'Why does Heaven not send down its power?
The great mandate has not been held fast.'
Now, what will the king do?"
The king said:
"Alas! Was I not born with a mandate from Heaven?"
Zǔyī returned, saying:
"Alas! Your crimes are many and listed above;
how can you demand a mandate from Heaven?
Yīn's approaching ruin
points to your deeds;
you will not escape destruction in your land."
Yīn had already mishandled Heaven's mandate.
Wēizǐ addressed the Grand Tutor and Junior Tutor.
Wēizǐ spoke thus:
"Grand Tutor, Junior Tutor,
will Yīn not perhaps bring order
to the four quarters?
Our ancestors achieved and displayed this above.
But we drown in wine below,
and through disorder ruin their virtue.
In Yīn, none, great or small,
but loves robbery and villainy;
ministers and officials act without measure,
and for all crimes,
there is no constant apprehension.
The common people rise up,
becoming enemies to each other.
Now Yīn is about to fall—
like wading a great river,
with no shore in sight.
Yīn's ruin has reached this day."
He said:
"Grand Tutor, Junior Tutor,
shall I set out in despair?
Our house is aged, retreating to the wilds.
Now you have no plan to tell me;
if we fall, what then shall we do?"
The Grand Tutor spoke thus:
"O prince, Heaven heavily
sends disaster to ruin the Yīn state,
and they are drowning in wine. They fear nothing,
opposing their elders
and former men of rank.
Now the Yīn people even steal the pure animals
of the gods and spirits for use,
and are tolerated, eating without disaster.
Heaven looks down on the Yīn people
governing them,
yet with enmity and exactions, summoning enemy hatred without cease.
Crimes gather into one,
with many sufferings and no redress.
Shāng now has disaster;
we rise to suffer its collapse.
If Shāng ruins its laws and perishes,
I will not be a subject or servant.
I advise the prince to leave and flee;
I long said, the child should be engraved;
if the prince does not leave,
we shall be utterly ruined.
Each must decide, each offer himself to the former kings;
I will not plan to flee."
In the eleventh year,
King Wǔ waged war against Yīn.
On the first month, day Wǔwǔ,
the army crossed at Mèngjīn.
Composed the three chapters of "The Great Declaration."
In the thirteenth year, in spring,
a grand assembly was held at Mèngjīn.
The King said:
Ah!
my friends and allied princes, and all you my officers,
listen clearly to my declaration!
Heaven and Earth are the parents of all creatures,
and of all creatures humanity is the most intelligent.
The one truly intelligent becomes the great sovereign;
the great sovereign is the parent of the people.
But now, King Shòu of Shāng
does not reverence Heaven above,
and inflicts calamities on the people below.
Abandoned to drunkenness and reckless in lust,
he has dared to exercise cruel oppression.
He has punished men through their families;
he has appointed offices through favoritism.
He has made palaces, towers, pavilions, embankments, ponds, and extravagant clothes,
to injure and harm you, the myriad families.
He has burned and roasted the loyal and good;
he has ripped open pregnant women.
August Heaven was moved with indignation,
and charged my deceased father Wén
reverently to execute its punishment;
but the great achievement was not completed.
I, the little child Fā,
with you, my friends and allied princes,
am going to inquire about the government of Shāng.
But Shòu has no repentant heart;
he sits squatting on his heels, not serving God nor the spirits of heaven and earth,
neglecting also the temple of his ancestors, and not sacrificing in it.
The victims and the vessels of millet all become the prey of wicked robbers.
Still he says,
'The people are mine; the decree is mine,'
never trying to check his insolence.
Heaven, protecting the inferior people,
made for them rulers,
and made for them instructors,
that they might be able to be aiding to God,
and secure the tranquillity of the four quarters.
In the question of who are guilty and who are not,
how dare I give any allowance to my own wishes?
With the same power we estimate their virtue; with the same virtue we estimate their righteousness.
Shòu has hundreds of thousands and millions of ministers,
but they have hundreds of thousands and millions of minds;
I have three thousand ministers,
but they have one mind.
The iniquity of Shāng is full;
Heaven gives command to destroy it.
If I did not comply with Heaven, my iniquity would be as great.
I, the little child, early and late am filled with apprehensions.
I have received the charge of my deceased father Wén;
I have offered special sacrifice to God;
I have performed the due services to the great Earth;
and I lead you, my hosts, to execute the punishment appointed by Heaven.
Heaven compassionates the people.
What the people desire,
Heaven will be found to give effect to.
Do you aid me, the One man,
to cleanse for ever all within the four seas.
Now is the time!—It may not be lost.
On Wǔwǔ,
the King halted on the north of the river,
when all the princes with their hosts were assembled.
The King then made a progress through the army, and made a declaration, saying,
Ah! ye multitudes of the western region,
hearken all to my words.
I have heard that the good man, doing good,
finds the day insufficient;
and that the evil man, doing evil,
also finds the day insufficient.
Now Shòu, the king of Shāng,
with strength pursues his lawless way.
He drives away the time-worn servants;
he associates with the criminals;
he is given to drink, and abandons himself to cruelty;
and his ministers have become changed by him.
They form parties and become enemies.
Oppressing and destroying one another by the power which they have,
the innocent cry to Heaven.
The foulness of Shòu's character is heard on high.
Heaven loves the people,
and the sovereign should reverently carry out this mind.
Xià's sovereign Jié could not follow the example of Heaven,
but sent forth his poisonous injuries through the states of the kingdom:
—Heaven therefore gave its aid to Chéng Tāng,
and charged him to discharge the appointment of Xià.
But Shòu's crimes exceed those of Jié.
He has degraded from office the greatly good;
he has behaved with cruel tyranny to his reprovers and helpers.
He says that with him is the appointment of Heaven;
he says that reverence is not worth while;
he says that sacrifice is of no use;
he says that tyranny is no harm.
The beacon for his looking at is not far off;—it is that king of Xià.
It would seem that Heaven is going by means of me to rule the people.
My dreams coincide with my divinations;
the auspicious omen is double.
My attack on Shāng must succeed.
Shòu has hundreds of thousands and millions of ordinary men,
divided in heart and divided in practice;
I have of ministers, able to govern, ten men,
one in heart and one in practice.
However numerous may be his relatives,
they are not equal to my virtuous men.
The people's errors are on my head.
'Now, I must go forward.'
'I will give display to my martial might,'
'enter his territories,'
'and take the evil oppressor.'
'My punishment of him will be more illustrious than that of Tāng.'
'Rouse yourselves, my heroes!'
Do not think that he is not to be feared;
better think that we are not equal to him.
The people are in trembling anxiety,
as if they were appealing to us to support them.
Oh! Unite your energies, unite your hearts;
so shall you forthwith establish your merit;
and you will for ever be held in reverence by your descendants.
At this time, the next day,
the King went round his six hosts in state,
and made a clear declaration to all his officers.
He said,
Oh! my valiant men of the western region,
Heaven has its evident principles,
and their requirements are clear.
But now Shāng's king Shòu
treats with contemptuous disregard the five constant virtues,
and idly abandons himself to wild idleness and irreverence.
He has cut himself off from Heaven,
and brought enmity between himself and the people.
He cut through the leg-bones of those who were crossing the river in the morning;
he ripped open the heart of the worthy man.
So he has exercised his terrible power,
poisoning and injuring all within the four seas.
His honors and confidence are given to the villainous and bad;
he has driven from him his instructors and guardians.
He has thrown aside the constant laws of nature;
he has imprisoned and enslaved the upright officer.
He neglects the sacrifices to heaven and earth;
he does not offer his offerings in the ancestral temple.
He makes contrivances of wonderful device and extraordinary cunning to please his woman.
God will not comply with his ways,
but sends down this time of his ruin.
Do you with untiring zeal support me, the One man,
reverently to execute the punishment appointed by Heaven.
The ancients have said,
'He who soothes us is our sovereign; he who oppresses us is our enemy.'
This solitary fellow Shòu, having exercised great tyranny,
is your perpetual enemy.
'It is well to foster virtue, and the well-being will be great;'
'in removing evil, strive to do it thoroughly.'
So I, the little child, with you, my hosts,
will utterly exterminate your enemy.
Do you, my hosts, press forward with decided firmness,
to sustain your sovereign.
Where there is much merit, there shall be large reward;
where you do not advance, there shall be conspicuous disgrace.
Oh! The virtue of my deceased father Wén was like the shining of the sun and moon.
His brightness extended over the four quarters of the land,
and shone signally in the western region.
Hence it is that our Zhōu has received the allegiance of many states.
If I conquer Shòu,
it is not because of my valor,
but because of my father Wén having no fault.
If Shòu conquer me,
it is not because my father Wén has any fault,
but because I, the little child, am not good.
King Wǔ had three hundred chariots of war,
and three hundred tiger-like warriors.
He fought with Shòu at Mùyě.
He made "The Declaration at Mù."
At the dawn of the jiazi day,
the king arrived at the outskirts of Shāng, Mùyě,
and there made his pledge.
The king held a yellow battle-axe in his left hand
and a white yak-tail banner in his right to command.
He said:
"Far have you come, people of the western lands!"
The king said:
"Ah! My allied rulers of friendly states,
and officers in charge: Minister of the Masses,
Minister of War, Minister of Works,
deputy commanders, brigade leaders, and division commanders,
leaders of thousands and leaders of hundreds,
and men of Yōng, Shǔ, Qiāng, Máo, Wēi, Lú, Péng, and Pú.
Raise your spears,
align your shields,
set up your lances,
and I will make my pledge."
The king said:
"The ancients had a saying:
'A hen does not crow at dawn.
If a hen crows at dawn, it brings ruin to the household.'
Now King Shòu of Shāng follows only the words of women.
He recklessly abandons the sacrifices he should offer
and does not respond to them;
he recklessly discards his own paternal
and maternal uncles
and does not employ them.
Instead, he honors and promotes
the fugitives from all quarters laden with crimes,
trusts and employs them,
making them high officials and ministers;
he lets them oppress the common people,
and commit treacheries in the capital of Shāng.
Now I, Fā, am only respectfully carrying out Heaven's punishment.
In today's battle,
do not exceed six or seven steps
before halting to regroup.
Be valiant, my warriors!
Do not strike more than four,
five,
six,
or seven times
before halting to regroup.
Be valiant, my warriors!
Be majestic and awe-inspiring,
like tigers,
like pí beasts,
like bears,
like brown bears,
on the outskirts of Shāng.
Do not attack those who flee to surrender,
but let them serve our western lands.
Be valiant, my warriors!
If you are not valiant,
you will bring death upon yourselves!"
King Wǔ attacked Yīn.
He went to attack. Returning, he disbanded the troops
and attended to the government affairs.
He composed the "Wǔchéng."
"In the first month, on the rénchén day,
when the moon was waning,
the next day, guǐsì,
the king set out from Zhōu on foot,
to march and attack Shāng."
In the fourth month,
when the moon began to shine,
the king came back from Shāng,
arriving at Fēng.
Then he laid aside arms and cultivated the arts of peace,
"returning the horses to the south of Huàshān,
and releasing the oxen in the fields of Táolín,
showing the world they would not be used again."
On the dīngwèi day,
he sacrificed in the ancestral temple of Zhōu,
and the lords of the states and domains
hurried busily,
holding the sacrificial vessels.
Three days later,
on the gēngxū day,
he offered burnt offerings and gazed afar,
greatly announcing the completion of the military campaign.
After the moon began to wax,
the rulers of various states and all the officials
received their mandates from Zhōu.
The king spoke thus:
"Alas!
O numerous lords!
Our former king founded the state and opened up the territory,
Gōngliǔ was able to solidify the achievements of the past,
down to Tàiwáng, who laid the foundation of the royal enterprise,
and Wángjì diligently served the royal house.
My cultured father, King Wén, was able to complete his merit,
greatly received the Mandate of Heaven,
to pacify all Xià.
"The great states feared his power,
the small states cherished his virtue."
Only in the ninth year,
the great unity was not yet achieved.
I, the little child, have inherited his will,
exposed the crimes of Shāng,
and reported to the great Heaven and Earth, and all the famous mountains and great rivers I passed.
I said:
'I, the principled great-grandson, King Fā of Zhōu,
am about to bring rectification to Shāng.
Now King Shòu of Shāng is without principle,
recklessly destroying the natural creations,
harming and oppressing the masses,
"being the haven for the fugitives of the world,
the gathering pool and den."
I, the little child, having obtained humane men,
dare to reverently follow the Lord on High,
to stop the chaos and violence.
All within Huáxià and beyond, barbarians included,
none do not follow and obey,
respectfully fulfilling Heaven's accomplished mandate.
"Thus I marched east,
to comfort their men and women.
These men and women
brought their black and yellow silks in baskets,
to show their allegiance to me, the King of Zhōu.
Heaven's favor shook them,
so they attached themselves to our great state Zhōu.'
O you spirits,
may you still assist me, to save the millions of people,
and not bring shame upon the spirits.
"On the wùwǔ day, the army crossed Mèngjīn."
On the guǐhài day, they arrayed at the outskirts of Shāng,
awaiting Heaven's favorable command.
At dawn on the jiǎzǐ day,
Shòu led "his troops, dense as a forest,
to meet at Mùyě."
None could withstand our army.
The front ranks turned their weapons,
attacking those behind, causing a rout.
"Blood flowed enough to float pestles,"
"with one military action,
the world was greatly settled."
Then he reversed the governance of Shāng,
restoring the old ways.
He freed Jīzǐ from imprisonment,
erected a mound over Bǐgān's tomb,
and paid respect at Shāngróng's village gate.
He distributed the wealth from the Lùtái tower,
opened the granaries of Jùqiáo to dispense grain,
greatly bestowed gifts throughout the land,
and the myriad families were pleased and submitted.
He established five ranks of nobility,
divided the land into three shares,
appointed officials based on worthiness,
and assigned positions according to ability.
He emphasized the five teachings for the people,
focusing on food, mourning, and sacrifice.
He honored good faith and clarified righteousness,
exalted virtue and rewarded merit,
governing the world with folded hands and ease.
King Wǔ, having defeated Yīn,
killed Shòu,
set up Wǔgēng,
and brought Jīzǐ back with him.
He composed the "Hóngfàn."
In the thirteenth year,
the king visited Jīzǐ.
The king then said:
"Alas!
Jīzǐ.
Heaven secretly secures the people below,
harmonizing their dwellings,
but I do not know the proper order of the constant principles."
Jīzǐ then replied:
"I have heard that in the past,
Gǔn dammed the floodwaters,
disturbing the arrangement of the Five Phases.
The Lord then became enraged,
not granting him the Nine Categories of the Great Plan,
and the constant principles were disrupted.
Gǔn was then executed and died,
and Yǔ succeeded and rose.
Heaven then bestowed upon Yǔ the Nine Categories of the Great Plan,
and the constant principles were properly ordered.
The first is called the Five Phases,
the second is called reverently practicing the Five Matters,
the third is called diligently applying the Eight Governmental Offices,
the fourth is called harmoniously using the Five Calendrical Periods,
the fifth is called establishing and using the Royal Ultimate,
the sixth is called governing with the Three Virtues,
the seventh is called clearly using the Examination of Doubts,
the eighth is called thoughtfully using the Various Verifications,
the ninth is called encouraging with the Five Blessings,
and awing with the Six Extremes."
I. The Five Elements:
The first is water,
the second is fire,
the third is wood,
the fourth is metal,
the fifth is earth.
Water is said to moisten and descend;
fire is said to blaze and ascend;
wood is said to bend and straighten;
metal is said to obey and change;
earth is said to sow and reap.
Moistening and descending produces saltiness;
blazing and ascending produces bitterness;
bending and straightening produces sourness;
obeying and changing produces acridity;
sowing and reaping produces sweetness.
II. The Five Affairs:
The first is demeanor,
the second is speech,
the third is vision,
the fourth is hearing,
the fifth is thought.
Demeanor should be respectful;
speech should be compliant;
vision should be clear;
hearing should be acute;
thought should be profound.
Respectfulness leads to solemnity;
compliance leads to order;
clarity leads to discernment;
acuteness leads to consultation;
profundity leads to sageliness.
III. The Eight Governmental Affairs:
The first is food,
the second is goods,
the third is sacrifices,
the fourth is public works,
the fifth is education,
the sixth is justice,
the seventh is reception of guests,
the eighth is military affairs.
IV. The Five Calendrical Measures:
The first is the year, the second is the month,
the third is the day, the fourth is the stars and planets,
the fifth is the calendrical calculations.
V. The Sovereign Standard:
The sovereign establishes the standard,
gathers the five blessings,
and bestows them upon the people.
Only then do the people turn to your standard,
and you preserve the standard.
Among all the people,
there should be no illicit cliques,
and no one should form biased virtues;
only the sovereign establishes the standard.
Among all the people,
those who have plans, actions, and integrity,
you should remember them.
Those who do not conform to the standard,
but are not guilty of offenses,
the sovereign should accept them.
If they appear content and say,
"I love virtue,"
you should bestow blessings upon them;
then these people will uphold the sovereign's standard.
Do not oppress the solitary and helpless,
nor fear the eminent and illustrious.
Those who have abilities and achievements,
encourage them to advance their conduct,
and the state will prosper.
Among all officials,
if they are already wealthy and virtuous,
but you cannot make them contribute to your household,
then these people are at fault.
If they have no goodwill,
even if you bestow blessings upon them,
they will bring you harm.
Do not be partial or biased;
follow the king's righteousness;
do not have personal preferences;
follow the king's way;
do not have personal aversions;
follow the king's path.
Without partiality or factionalism,
the king's way is broad and level;
without factionalism or partiality,
the king's way is peaceful and even;
without deviation or obliquity,
the king's way is upright and straight.
Gather at the standard,
and return to the standard.
The words expounding the sovereign standard
are constant and instructive,
following the instruction of the Lord.
All the people,
regarding the expounded words of the standard,
should instruct and practice them,
to draw near to the Son of Heaven's brilliance.
It is said the Son of Heaven acts as the parent of the people,
and thus becomes the king of all under heaven.
VI. The Three Virtues:
The first is uprightness and correctness,
the second is firmness and mastery,
the third is gentleness and mastery.
In peace and tranquility, be upright and correct.
Against the unyielding and unfriendly, use firmness and mastery;
with the harmonious and friendly, use gentleness and mastery.
For the deep and hidden, use firmness and mastery;
for the eminent and illustrious, use gentleness and mastery.
Only the ruler may confer blessings,
only the ruler may exercise authority,
only the ruler may enjoy fine food;
ministers should not confer blessings, exercise authority, or enjoy fine food.
If ministers confer blessings, exercise authority,
or enjoy fine food,
it will harm your household,
and bring misfortune to your state.
People will become biased and perverse,
and the common people will transgress and err.
VII. Examining Doubts:
Select and appoint diviners.
Then command the divination:
called rain, called clearing,
called overcast, called
mist, called overcoming,
called the upright hexagram, called the changing hexagram,
in all seven. Of the turtle shell divinations, five;
of the stalk divinations, two;
deduce the discrepancies.
Appoint these persons as diviners;
if three persons divine,
then follow the words of two.
If you have great doubts,
consult your own mind,
consult the high officials and nobles,
consult the common people,
consult the turtle shell and stalk divinations.
If you consent,
the turtle shell consents, the stalks consent,
the high officials and nobles consent, the common people consent,
this is called great unanimity.
Your person will be healthy and strong,
and your descendants will be fortunate and auspicious.
If you consent,
the turtle shell consents, the stalks consent,
but the high officials and nobles oppose, the common people oppose,
it is auspicious.
If the high officials and nobles consent,
the turtle shell consents, the stalks consent,
but you oppose, the common people oppose,
it is auspicious.
If the common people consent,
the turtle shell consents, the stalks consent,
but you oppose, the high officials and nobles oppose,
it is auspicious.
If you consent,
the turtle shell consents, but the stalks oppose,
the high officials and nobles oppose, the common people oppose,
for internal affairs, auspicious;
for external affairs, inauspicious.
If both the turtle shell and stalks oppose the human will,
inaction brings auspiciousness;
action brings inauspiciousness.
VIII. Various Signs:
They are rain, sunshine, heat, cold,
wind, and timeliness.
When these five are fully present,
each in its proper order,
the various plants grow lush and abundant.
If one is excessive, it is inauspicious;
if one is absent, it is inauspicious.
The auspicious signs:
Solemnity brings timely rain;
order brings timely sunshine;
discernment brings timely heat;
consultation brings timely cold;
sageliness brings timely wind.
The inauspicious signs:
Arrogance brings constant rain;
transgression brings constant sunshine;
indolence brings constant heat;
haste brings constant cold;
ignorance brings constant wind.
It is said the king's inspection is like the year,
the high officials and nobles like the month,
the officers like the day.
If the year, month, and day are unchanging,
the hundred grains will ripen,
governance will be enlightened,
outstanding people will be prominent,
and the household will be peaceful and prosperous.
If the day, month, and year change,
the hundred grains will not ripen,
governance will be dark and unenlightened,
outstanding people will be obscure,
and the household will be unsettled and troubled.
The common people are like stars,
some stars favor wind,
some stars favor rain.
The sun and moon in their courses
bring winter and summer.
When the moon follows the stars,
it brings wind and rain.
Nine. The Five Blessings:
first, longevity;
second, wealth;
third, health and tranquility;
fourth, cultivation of virtuous character;
fifth, a peaceful death.
The Six Calamities:
first, untimely death;
second, sickness;
third, sorrow;
fourth, poverty;
fifth, wickedness;
sixth, weakness."
After King Wǔ defeated the Yīn,
he enfeoffed the nobles,
distributed the ancestral vessels,
and composed "The Distribution of Vessels."
The Western Lǚ tribe presented hounds.
The Grand Guardian composed "The Hounds of Lǚ."
"Having conquered Shāng,
they opened roads to the nine Yí and eight Mán tribes."
The Western Lǚ tribe sent their hounds as tribute.
The Grand Guardian then composed "The Hounds of Lǚ,"
to instruct the king.
He said:
"Alas!
When a wise king is careful about virtue,
all the barbarian tribes submit.
Regardless of distance,
all present their local products,
which are for clothing, food, and utensils.
The king then displays virtue
to states of different surnames,
not neglecting their duties.
'He distributes precious jades among the states of uncles and brothers,
thereby showing affection.'
'People do not change the things,
but virtue makes them valuable.'
When virtue is abundant, one does not treat others lightly or insult them.
If you insult gentlemen,
you cannot win their hearts;
if you insult common people,
you cannot get their full effort.
Do not be enslaved by sights and sounds,
and all measures will be correct.
Toying with people loses virtue,
toying with things loses ambition.
Ambition is settled by the Way,
words are guided by the Way.
Do not do useless things to harm the useful,
then achievements will be made;
do not value exotic things and despise the practical,
then the people will be content.
Do not keep dogs or horses not native to the land,
nor rear rare birds and strange beasts in the state;
do not treasure distant things,
then distant people will submit;
if you treasure only the worthy,
then nearby people will be at peace.
Alas!
Day and night, never be idle.
If you do not attend to small details,
eventually you will impair great virtue.
To build a mound nine ren high,
the work may fail for lack of one basket of earth.
If you truly follow this,
the people will preserve their homes,
and you will reign for generations."
Cháo Bó came to court.
Ruì Bó composed "The Charge to the Cháo Envoy."
King Wǔ fell ill.
The Duke of Zhōu composed "The Metal-Bound Coffer."
In the second year after conquering Shāng,
the king was ill and uneasy.
The two dukes said:
"Shall we reverently divine for the king?"
The Duke of Zhōu said:
"We must not distress our former kings."
The Duke then took it upon himself as his task,
building three altars on one cleared ground.
He set up an altar facing north in the south,
and the Duke of Zhōu stood there.
Holding a jade disc and grasping a jade tablet,
he addressed King Tài,
King Jì, and King Wén.
The scribe then read the prayer:
"Your eldest grandson,
has encountered a severe and vicious illness.
If you three kings
truly have the duty in heaven
to protect him,
let Dàn take his place.
I am kind and clever,
versatile and skilled,
capable of serving the spirits.
Your eldest grandson is not as versatile and skilled as Dàn,
and cannot serve the spirits.
He received the mandate in the court of Di,
to spread protection over the four quarters,
thus able to settle your descendants on the earth below;
the people of the four quarters
all revere him.
Alas!
Do not let fall the precious mandate from heaven,
so our former kings may also have eternal support.
Now I await your command through the great tortoise.
If you grant my request,
I will take the jade disc and tablet
back, awaiting your order;
if you do not grant it,
I will put away the disc and tablet."
Then they divined with three tortoises,
all consistently auspicious.
Opening the bamboo tubes
to examine the writings,
they were all auspicious.
The Duke said:
"The omens! The king
will come to no harm.
I have newly received the mandate
from the three kings,
and only seek its eternal endurance.
Here I await,
hoping you will remember me."
The Duke returned,
and placed the document in the metal-bound coffer.
The king recovered the next day.
After King Wǔ's death,
Guǎn Shū and his brothers
spread rumors in the state, saying:
"The Duke will do harm to the young king."
The Duke of Zhōu then told the two dukes:
"If I do not take action,
I will have nothing to report to our former kings."
The Duke of Zhōu resided in the east for two years,
and the criminals were captured.
Afterwards,
the Duke composed a poem to present to the king,
titled "The Owl."
The king still did not dare to blame the Duke.
In autumn, when the grain was ripe,
but not yet harvested,
heaven sent great thunder, lightning, and wind;
the grain all fell down,
and large trees were uprooted.
The people were greatly terrified,
and the king and his officials donned court robes
to open the metal-bound coffer and read the document,
thus learning of the Duke's
offer to take it upon himself
to substitute for King Wǔ.
The two dukes and the king
then questioned the scribes and various officials,
who replied:
"It is true. Alas! The Duke ordered us not to speak."
The king held the document and wept, saying:
"There is no need for reverent divination.
In the past, the Duke labored for the royal house,
but I, a young person, did not know.
Now heaven has moved in majesty
to display the Duke's virtue.
I, the young king, should personally go to welcome him anew,
for the rites of our state also require it."
The king went out to the suburbs,
and heaven rained, the wind reversed,
and the grain all stood up.
The two dukes ordered the people
to prop up all the fallen large trees,
and they all stood firm.
That year, there was a great harvest.
After King Wǔ's death,
the Three Supervisors and the Huái Yí rebelled,
and the Duke of Zhōu, assisting King Chéng,
intended to suppress the Yīn.
He composed "The Great Announcement."
The king spoke thus:
"I announce to you,
the many states,
and your officers.
Unfortunate!
Heaven has sent down calamities upon our house,
without respite! I, the young king,
have inherited the boundless great heritage and duties.
Not having created wisdom
to guide the people to well-being,
how much less should it be said that
I am able to comprehend the Mandate of Heaven?
Alas! I, the young son,
feel as if treading deep water;
I only seek the means by which I may cross over.
Display the tortoise shell,
display the mandate received by former kings,
so as not to forget the great achievements!
I dare not conceal the awe-inspiring use of Heaven's decrees.
King Wén left us the great precious tortoise,
to continue the bright mandate of Heaven.
I approached it for an oracle, and it said:
'There is great hardship in the western lands,
the people of the western lands are also restless,
and now they are stirring up trouble.'
The petty remnant of Yīn,
daringly attempts to restore their order.
Heaven sends down awe,
knowing that our state has flaws,
and the people are not at peace,
saying:
'We shall restore,'
turning to despise our state of Zhōu.
Now they are stirring,
now on the following day.
There are ten worthy men among the people
to assist me, in order to complete the achievements planned by King Wén and King Wǔ.
We have great affairs and auspiciousness;
my divinations are all favorable!
Therefore I announce to the rulers of our friendly states,
and to the officials,
the multitude of officers,
and the administrators, saying:
'I have obtained auspicious divinations;
I intend to lead you, the multitude of states,
to attack the fugitive ministers of Yīn.'
You, rulers of the multitude of states,
and you multitude of officers and administrators,
all without exception objected, saying:
'The hardship is great, the people are not tranquil.
Moreover, it is in the king's palace and the mansions of the state rulers,
and even we, the young sons and our elders,
cannot undertake the campaign;
why should the king not disregard the divination?'
Therefore I, the young one, deeply ponder the difficulty, saying:
Alas! Truly, turmoil
brings sorrow to the widowers and widows!
I, created for Heaven's service, am left with
great and heavy burdens cast upon my person,
and I, the young one, do not merely pity myself.
It is right that you, rulers of states,
and you multitude of officers, officials, and administrators,
comfort me, saying:
'Do not be overwhelmed by pity;
you must not fail to complete the achievements planned by your tranquil father.'
Enough! I, the young son,
dare not disregard the command of God.
Heaven showed favor to King Wén,
and raised our small state of Zhōu.
King Wén used divination,
and was able to peacefully receive this mandate.
Now Heaven is assisting the people;
how much more should we also use divination?
Alas! The bright terror of Heaven
supports our great foundation!'
The king said: "You are the old ministers,
you can well recall the distant past;
do you know how King Wén toiled?
Heaven secretly guided us to the place of success;
I dare not but fully complete the affairs planned by King Wén.
Therefore I greatly exhort and guide the rulers of our friendly states;
Heaven's sincere words assist us,
it examines our people;
how should I not
bring to an end the achievements planned by the former tranquil men?
Heaven also uses toil to admonish our people,
as if they had an illness;
how dare I not bring to completion
the blessings received by the former tranquil men!"
The king said:
"As in former times, I shall go forth;
I speak of hardship, thinking of it daily.
If a father builds a house,
having laid the foundation,
and his son is unwilling to raise the hall,
how much less will he complete the structure?
If a father clears the land,
and his son is unwilling to sow,
how much less will he reap?
Would that father then say:
'I have a successor who will not abandon the foundation'?
Therefore, how dare I not
personally complete the great mandate of King Wén?
If an elder brother dies,
and there are friends attacking his son,
would the people who nurture him encourage and not rescue him?"
The king said:
"Alas! Take action! You, rulers of the multitude of states,
and you administrators.
Enlightening the state depends on the wise;
there are also these ten men
who guide and know the mandate of God.
As for Heaven's sincere assistance,
you at that time did not dare to change the laws;
how much less now that Heaven has sent down calamity upon the state of Zhōu?
Only the great troublemakers,
daringly allied and attacked within their own house;
you also do not know that the Mandate of Heaven is not easily obtained!
I deeply reflect, saying:
Heaven wishes to destroy Yīn; like a farmer,
how dare I not complete my field?
Heaven also shows favor to the former tranquil men;
how can I resort to divination to the utmost?
Dare I not follow?
Should I lead the tranquil men
to possess the designated territory?
Moreover, now the divinations are all auspicious;
therefore I greatly lead you eastward on campaign.

go and exhaust your heart,

appease the unappeased,

in your duties, should broaden

himself doing what is unlawful;
though his crime is small,

The king said:

use their righteous punishments and righteous killings,

The king said:

a father who cannot love his son

'You should quickly use King Wén's punishments,

how much more the external junior sons and instructors,

down to minor officers and various bailiffs;

Enough!

if they cannot govern their families,
and their minor officers and external officials,
are only tyrannical and cruel,
greatly abandoning the king's command;
this is not governing with virtue.

and thereby guide the people;
only King Wén's reverence and caution,
thus guided the people.
Saying:
'I only seek to follow.'
