could truly display their talents.
Strictly following the great model, he could employ the three appointments
and the three talents.
In the capital of Shāng,
they harmonized within the city;
in the four quarters,
they greatly displayed virtue through the model.
Ah! As for Shòu, in his character he was brutal,
associating with those who glorified punishment and were violent in character,
throughout his state;
and he gathered those accustomed to idle virtues,
throughout his government.
The Lord on High severely punished him,
and caused us, the people of Xià,
to replace Shāng and receive the mandate,
universally governing the myriad clans.
Then King Wén and King Wǔ,
were able to know the hearts of the three appointments,
and clearly see the hearts of the three talents;
they reverently served the Lord on High,
and established leaders and elders for the people.
They established the government:
the appointers, judges, and pastors, forming the three affairs.
The tiger guards, robe attendants, grooms, and minor officers,
the personal attendants, and the various offices and storehouses.
The great and small city chiefs,
the artisans, external ministers, and various officers,
the grand historians, chief officers, and the many constant good officers.
The ministers of works, war, and lands, the assistants, and multitudes.
The Yí, Mǐ, Lú, and Zhēng tribes. The three Bó and Bǎn officials.
King Wén was able to settle their hearts,
and thus could establish these constant officers and managers of the people,
to employ the talented and virtuous.
King Wén did not presume to interfere
with various opinions.
As for various legal cases and cautious matters,
only the officials and stewards
were instructed on what to follow or avoid. Regarding various legal cases and cautious matters,
King Wén did not dare to involve himself in these.
Moreover, King Wǔ followed and completed the achievements,
not daring to abandon their righteous virtue;
he followed and considered the accommodating virtue,
thereby jointly receiving this great foundation.
Alas! The young son is now king!
From now on, we shall establish governance and manage affairs.
For judges and stewards,
we must be able to clearly understand their suitability,
then let them bring order;
assist us in receiving the people,
and harmonize our various legal cases and cautious matters.
At such times, do not interfere,
not even with a single word or utterance.
Then we shall ultimately have virtuous and talented men,
to govern the people we have received.
Alas! I, Dàn,
having received the fine words of others,
have fully informed the young king!
From now on, the cultured sons and cultured grandsons,
must not err in various legal cases and cautious matters,
but let the proper officials govern them.
Since ancient times, the Shāng people,
and also our Zhōu King Wén,
in establishing governance and managing affairs: for stewards and judges,
were able to position them appropriately,
and could follow and extend them,
thus enabling governance.
In the state, there should be no establishment of governance
using petty men,
who are not guided by virtue,
for this does not manifest glory in their era.
From now on in establishing governance,
do not use petty men,
but only employ good men
to diligently assist our state and family.
Now, cultured sons and cultured grandsons,
the young son is king.
Do not err in various legal cases,
but leave them to the officials and stewards.
You should discipline your armies,
to tread in the footsteps of Yǔ.
March throughout the world,
reaching beyond the seas,
with none who do not submit.
Thereby behold King Wén's brilliant light,
and propagate King Wǔ's great achievements.
Alas! From now on, when later kings establish governance,
they must be able to employ constant virtuous men."
The Duke of Zhōu spoke thus:
"Grand Historian!
Minister of Justice, Sū Gōng! Model
reverence in your handling of legal cases,
to nurture our royal state.
This model requires caution,
to apply penalties with fairness."
King Chéng, having ended the Shāng mandate,
and subdued the Huáiyí,
returned to Fēng.
He composed the "Zhōu Guān".
The Zhōu king pacified the myriad states,
toured the marquises and earls,
campaigned against those not submissive,
and comforted the millions of people.
The rulers of the six domains
all received his virtue.
Returning to the ancestral Zhōu,
he supervised and rectified the governing officials.
The king said:
"As in the great plans of old,
establish order before chaos arises,
secure the state before danger appears.
It is said:
Táng and Yú looked to antiquity,
establishing only a hundred offices;
internally, there were the chief minister and the four peaks,
externally, there were regional stewards and feudal lords.
All governance was harmonious,
'and the myriad states were all tranquil'.
In Xià and Shāng, offices doubled,
yet they could still achieve order.
An enlightened king establishes governance,
not focusing on the number of offices,
but on the quality of the people.
Now I, the young son,
reverently diligent in virtue,
strive day and night yet feel inadequate.
Looking up, I follow the examples of former times
as instruction,
to guide these offices.
'Establish the Grand Preceptor, Grand Mentor, and Grand Guardian,
these are the Three Dukes.'
They deliberate on the Way and manage the state,
harmonizing Yīn and Yáng.
'Offices need not be fully staffed,
but only with the right people.'
'The Junior Preceptor, Junior Mentor, and Junior Guardian,
are called the Three Solitaries.'
They assist the dukes in broadening transformation,
reverently illuminating heaven and earth,
and aiding me, the one man.
The Prime Minister oversees the state's governance,
commands all officials,
and balances the four seas.
The Minister of Education oversees the state's instruction,
spreads the five codes,
and harmonizes the millions of people.
The Minister of Rites oversees the state's ceremonies,
serves the spirits and men,
and harmonizes high and low.
The Minister of War oversees the state's military,
commands the six armies,
and pacifies the state and its territories.
The Minister of Justice oversees the state's prohibitions,
investigates the wicked and crafty,
and punishes the violent and disorderly.
The Minister of Works oversees the state's lands,
settles the four classes of people,
and times the benefits of the land.
The six ministers divide their duties,
each leading their subordinates
to guide the nine regions,
enriching and completing the lives of the millions.
Every six years,
the five domains come to court once.
After another six years,
the king then tours accordingly.
He examines the institutions at the four peaks,
where the feudal lords each court at the regional peaks,
greatly clarifying promotions and demotions.
The king said:
"Alas!
All you noblemen with offices,
revere your duties,
be cautious in issuing orders,
for orders once issued must be carried out,
not reversed.
With public spirit eliminating private interests,
the people will truly cherish you.
Study antiquity to enter office,
'deliberate on affairs with regulation',
and governance will not go astray.
Let the classic norms be your teacher,
and do not use glib talk to confuse your office.
Harboring doubts ruins plans,
negligence and neglect disrupt governance,
not studying is like facing a wall,
and handling affairs will only bring trouble.
Admonish you, ministers and officers:
high achievement comes from ambition,
broad enterprise comes from diligence,
only with decisive judgment
will there be no future difficulties.
Position does not invite arrogance,
emolument does not invite extravagance.
Reverence and frugality are virtue,
'do not practice deceit'.
Cultivating virtue,
the heart is at ease and days are blessed;
practicing deceit,
the heart is labored and days become clumsy.
'In favor, think of danger',
there is nothing not to be revered,
'if you do not fear, you will enter fear'.
Pushing forth the worthy and yielding to the able,
then the various officials will be harmonious;
without harmony, governance becomes chaotic.
Recommending those capable for office,
is your ability;
appointing the unsuitable,
is your failure.
The king said:
"Alas!
'Three affairs and the great officers',
revere your offices,
order your governance,
to assist your sovereign,
eternally comfort the millions of people,
and the myriad states will not be wearied."
King Chéng, having campaigned against the Eastern Yí,
the Sùshèn came to congratulate,
and the king had Róng Bó compose the "Decree on Rewarding the Sùshèn".
The Duke of Zhōu was in Fēng,
about to pass away,
wishing to be buried in Chéngzhōu.
The duke died,
King Chéng buried him in Bì,
and announced it to the Duke of Zhōu.
He composed the "Bógū".
After the Duke of Zhōu passed away,
the king commanded Jūn Chén to govern and bring order to the eastern suburb of Chéngzhōu.
Thus, the chapter "Jūn Chén" was composed.
The king spoke thus:
Jūn Chén!
You possess the virtuous qualities of filial piety and reverence.
"Only through filial piety and friendship toward brothers,
can one extend these to governance."
I command you to administer this eastern suburb;
be reverent!
In the past, the Duke of Zhōu served as a teacher and protector to the myriad people,
and the people cherished his virtue.
Go and be cautious in your office,
following these constant principles,
diligently illuminating the instructions of the Duke of Zhōu,
so that the people may be well-governed.
I have heard it said:
The fragrance of perfect governance
reaches and moves the divine spirits.
"It is not the millet that has the fragrance;
bright virtue alone has the fragrance."
You should model yourself on the teachings and counsels of the Duke of Zhōu,
daily striving with diligence,
daring not to indulge in ease or pleasure.
"When people have not seen a sage,
it is as if they cannot see one;
having seen a sage,
they still cannot follow the sage."
Take warning!
"You are the wind,
the common people are the grass."
In planning your governance,
nothing should be without its difficulties.
There are things to abolish and things to promote;
"In coming and going, take counsel from your multitude,
and when the various opinions agree, deliberate upon them."
"When you have excellent plans and counsels,
report them to your sovereign within,
and then carry them out consistently abroad,
saying:
'These plans, these counsels
are due to the virtue of our sovereign.'
Alas!
If all ministers were thus,
how excellent and illustrious would it be!"
The king said:
Jūn Chén!
You must enlarge upon the great instructions of the Duke of Zhōu,
do not rely on power to display authority,
nor depend on laws to impose harshness.
Be lenient yet principled,
composed and harmonious.
When the people of Yīn are under punishment,
if I say punish,
you may choose not to punish;
if I say pardon,
you may choose not to pardon,
but seek the mean.
If any do not comply with your governance,
or are not transformed by your instructions,
punish to stop further offenses, then punish.
Those accustomed to villainy,
who ruin constant virtues and disturb customs,
even in small matters, do not pardon.
Do not be angry with the obstinate;
"do not expect perfection from any one person,"
"you must have forbearance,
then you will achieve success."
With tolerance,
virtue becomes great.
Select those who are virtuous,
and also distinguish those who may not be;
advance the good,
to lead those who are not good.
The nature of the people is originally sincere,
but it changes with circumstances.
They go against the commands from above,
following their own preferences.
If you can reverently uphold the statutes and rest in virtue,
then there will be none who do not change,
truly ascending to the great path.
Thus I will receive abundant blessings,
and your excellence
will be praised forever.
When King Chéng was about to die,
he commanded Duke Shào and Duke Bì to lead the feudal lords in assisting King Kāng.
Thus, the chapter "Gù Mìng" was composed.
In the fourth month,
on the first appearance of the waning moon,
the king was unwell.
On the jiǎzǐ day,
the king washed his hair and face
with water;
his attendants robed him in his cap and court dress,
and he leaned on a jade-adorned table.
Then he summoned together Grand Bǎofu Shì,
the Earl of Ruì, the Earl of Tóng, Duke Bì,
the Marquis of Wèi, Duke Máo, the Master of the Guards,
the Tiger Ministers, the hundred officers, and the various officials.
The king said:
"Alas! My illness has greatly progressed,
and is critical.
The ailment daily worsens,
and I am near the end.
Fearing I may not be able to speak my last charge on succession,
I now carefully instruct and command you.
In the past, our lords King Wén and King Wǔ
displayed a double brilliance, established the laws,
set forth instructions, which were practiced,
and practiced without deviation,
thus succeeding in overthrowing Yīn and receiving the great mandate.
I, the later simple one,
reverently met the terrors of Heaven,
succeeded in guarding the great instructions of Wén and Wǔ,
daring not to be heedless or transgress.
Now Heaven has sent down this illness and danger,
and I cannot rise or awaken.
You should clearly understand my words,
and with reverence protect my eldest son Zhāo,
broadly aiding him through difficulties.
Pacify the distant and be able with the near,
tranquilize and encourage the states, small and great.
Think how people bring disorder
through their demeanor;
do not let Zhāo rashly rush into what is not right."
Having received these commands, they withdrew,
and set out the king's robes in the court.
The next day, yǐchǒu, the king died.
The Grand Bǎofu ordered Zhòng Huán and Nángōng Máo
to assist
Marquis Qí Lǚ Jí, with two spears and halberds,
and a hundred tiger warriors, to meet Prince Zhāo
outside the southern gate;
they escorted him into the side chamber, where he dwelt as the mourning sovereign.
On the dīngmǎo day, orders were given for the preparation of the plan and regulations.
Seven days later, on the guǐyǒu day,
the chief minister ordered the officers to prepare the materials.
The attendants set up the axe-embroidered screen and the king's robes.
In the window space facing south, were spread doubled bamboo mats
with axe-embroidered edges,
and a table inlaid with beautiful jade.
In the western wall facing east,
were spread doubled fine reed mats with patterned edges,
and a table inlaid with patterned shell.
In the eastern wall facing west,
were spread doubled rich mats with painted edges,
and a table inlaid with carved jade.
In the western alcove facing south,
were spread doubled bamboo-strip mats with black silk edges,
and a lacquered table.
Five kinds of jade: the displayed treasures,
the red sword, the great instructions,
the large round scepter, and the curved scepters were in the western wall;
the great jade, the foreign jade,
the celestial sphere, and the Hé diagram
were in the eastern wall;
Yìn's dance costumes, the great shell, the great drum
were in the western chamber;
Duì's spear, Hé's bow,
and Chuí's bamboo arrows were in the eastern chamber.
The great carriage was placed facing the guest's steps,
the secondary carriage facing the eastern steps,
the first carriage in front of the left gate-house,
the next carriage in front of the right gate-house.
Two men in sparrow-plumed caps, holding three-bladed spears,
stood inside the Bì gate;
four men in dark blue caps, holding spears with blades upward,
flanked the steps on both sides;
one man in a ceremonial cap, holding a battle-axe,
stood in the eastern hall;
one man in a ceremonial cap, holding a broad-axe,
stood in the western hall;
one man in a ceremonial cap, holding a pointed lance,
stood at the eastern corner;
one man in a ceremonial cap, holding a three-edged lance,
stood at the western corner;
one man in a ceremonial cap, holding a sharp lance,
stood at the side steps.
The king, in a hemp cap and axe-embroidered skirt,
ascended by the guest's steps.
The ministers and feudal lords
in hemp caps and ant-colored skirts,
entered and took their positions.
The Grand Bǎofu, the Grand Historiographer, and the Grand Ancestral Minister
all wore hemp caps and red skirts.
The Grand Bǎofu held the great jade tablet,
the Assistant Minister
presented the cup and the mào scepter,
ascending by the eastern steps.
The Grand Historiographer held the document,
ascending by the guest's steps,
and respectfully read the king's charge.
It was said:
"The Empress, leaning on the jade table,
proclaimed the final command,
ordering you to inherit the instructions,
to rule over the state of Zhōu;
to follow the great laws,
harmonize all under heaven,
and thereby respond to and promote the illustrious teachings of King Wén and King Wǔ."
The King bowed twice,
and rose. He replied, saying:
"Insignificant as I am, the least of men,
how can I bring order to
the four quarters,
and revere and fear the majesty of Heaven?"
Then he received the tóng and mào,
the King advanced three times, made three offerings,
and stepped back three times. The
Zōng said: "Partake."
The Grand Guardian received the tóng,
descended, and washed his hands.
With a different tóng, he held a zhāng to make the toast.
He handed the tóng to the Zōngrén; bowed,
and the King returned the bow.
The Grand Guardian received the tóng, made an offering,
tasted it, and placed it down.
He handed the tóng to the Zōngrén, bowed,
and the King returned the bow.
The Grand Guardian descended.
The ceremony concluded.
The feudal lords exited the temple gate and waited.
King Kāng, having assumed the role of the Son of Heaven,
then addressed the feudal lords.
This became "The Announcement of King Kāng."
The King emerged within the Yìng Gate,
the Grand Guardian led the western feudal lords
to enter the left of the Yìng Gate,
Duke Bì led the eastern feudal lords
to enter the right of the Yìng Gate,
all displaying yellow and red carriages.
The guests presented jade tablets and gifts, saying:
"We, your servants and guards,
dare to offer local tributes."
All bowed twice and touched their heads to the ground.
King Yì, inheriting virtue, replied
with a bow.
The Grand Guardian and Ruì Bó
both advanced, exchanged bows,
and all bowed twice, touching their heads to the ground, saying:
"We dare to respectfully inform the Son of Heaven,
that August Heaven changed the mandate of the great state of Yīn,
and only Zhōu's King Wén and King Wǔ
greatly received its favor,
able to care for the western lands.
Only the newly ascended King,
fully harmonized rewards and punishments,
secured his achievements,
thereby spreading blessings to later generations.
Now, may the King be reverent!
Strengthen the six armies.
Do not ruin the solitary mandate of our High Ancestor."
The King spoke thus:
"Feudal lords of various states—Hóu, Diàn, Nán, and Wèi—
I, the one person, Zhào, respond to your address.
In the past, our rulers Wén and Wǔ greatly enriched and pacified,
not pursuing faults,
achieved utmost sincerity and trust,
thereby illuminating all under heaven.
Thus, there were also brave warriors,
ministers of undivided loyalty,
who protected and governed the royal house,
thereby receiving the correct mandate from the High God.
August Heaven thereby instructed in its way,
entrusted the four quarters,
and commanded the establishment of feudal lords and protective screens,
for us later generations.
Now, I, with my uncles,
still hope you will join and care,
continuing your ancestors' service to the former kings.
Though your persons are abroad,
your hearts are never absent from the royal house.
Thereby, support and care for this,
and do not leave this young son to shame."
The assembled dukes, having heard the command,
exchanged bows, hurried out,
and the King removed his ceremonial cap and returned to mourning attire.
King Kāng ordered the completion of the record,
divided dwelling areas,
and settled the suburbs of Chéngzhōu.
This became "The Charge to Duke Bì."
"In the twelfth year,
on the sixth month, day Gēngwǔ,
at the first appearance of the moon."
Three days later, on Rénshēn,
"The King walked in the morning from Zōngzhōu,
arriving at Fēng."
With the multitudes of Chéngzhōu,
he ordered Duke Bì to protect and govern the eastern suburbs.
The King spoke thus:
Alas!
Father and Master!
Only King Wén and King Wǔ spread great virtue throughout the land,
thereby able to receive the mandate of Yīn.
Only the Duke of Zhōu assisted the former king,
"securing and settling his house."
He cautioned the stubborn people of Yīn,
moved them to Luòyì,
close to the royal house,
to transform them through instruction.
Now, three generations have passed,
times have changed and customs shifted,
the four quarters are without trouble,
and I, the one person, am at peace.
The Way has its rises and falls,
governance must change with customs;
if goodness is not recognized as good,
the people have nothing to encourage them.
Only you, Duke, cultivate virtue,
are diligent in small matters,
have assisted four generations,
maintained dignity to lead subordinates,
and all have revered your words.
Your fine achievements surpass those of former kings,
and I, the young son, rely on your accomplishments with folded hands.
The King said:
Alas!
Father and Master!
Now I respectfully charge you with the tasks of the Duke of Zhōu.
Go forth!
"Distinguish the good from the evil,
mark out their dwellings."
"Praise the good and condemn the evil,"
"establish models and reputations."
For those not following the instructions,
separate their wells and boundaries,
to make them fear and aspire.
Redraw the suburban borders,
carefully secure the defenses,
to bring peace to the four seas.
Governance values constancy,
words should be essential,
not merely seeking novelty.
The customs of the merchants are frivolous,
clever speech is prized,
and remnants of this remain.
May you, Duke, keep this in mind!
I have heard it said:
Families long in privilege
seldom uphold ritual.
They indulge and override virtue,
truly opposing Heaven's Way.
Corrupted by extravagance and beauty,
through all ages it is the same;
these numerous officers of Yīn,
long accustomed to favor,
rely on excess and destroy righteousness,
flaunting finery.
Proud, dissolute, and boastful,
they will end in evil;
though their stray hearts be restrained,
to control them is difficult.
Wealth with ability to instruct
"leads to long life."
Only virtue and righteousness
are the great instructions.
Without following ancient teachings,
how can there be instruction?
The King said:
Alas!
Father and Master!
The safety or danger of the state
lies with these Yīn officers;
"neither too harsh nor too gentle,"
their virtue will be truly cultivated.
Only the Duke of Zhōu could carefully begin it,
only Jūn Chén could harmonize its middle,
and only you, Duke, can complete its end.
The three rulers united in heart,
all reached the Way.
Where the Way prevails, governance is ordered,
"moistening the people with kindness."
The four barbarians in left-fastened garments
all rely on it.
I, the young son, will long enjoy much happiness.
May you, Duke, at this time in Chéngzhōu
establish an endless foundation,
and gain endless renown.
Let your descendants follow this model,
and there will be good order.
Alas!
Do not say it cannot be done,
only exert your heart;
do not say the people are few,
only be careful in your tasks.
Reverently follow the accomplished deeds of the former kings,
to excel the governance of the past."
King Mù commanded Jūn Yá
to become the Grand Minister of Education of Zhōu.
The "Jūn Yá" was composed.
The king spoke thus:
"Alas!
Jūn Yá!
Your grandfather and father
through generations were steadfastly loyal and faithful,
served diligently the royal house,
and achieved merits,
which were recorded on the grand banner.
I, the young one, inherit and preserve the legacy of Wén, Wǔ, Chéng, and Kāng;
and also rely on the ministers of the former kings
to assist in governing the four quarters.
My heart is anxious and fearful,
as if treading on a tiger's tail,
or crossing the spring ice.
Now I command you to be my support,
to serve as my limbs and backbone.
Continue in your ancestral duties,
and do not disgrace your forefathers.
Widely promulgate the five constant virtues,
and harmonize the people's norms.
If your own person can be upright,
none will dare not to be upright.
The people's hearts lack a mean,
only you provide that mean.
'In summer's heat and rain,
the common people only complain and lament;
in winter's severe cold,
the common people also only complain and lament.'
Truly, it is hard!
Think of their hardships to plan for their ease,
and the people will be at peace.
Alas!
'How glorious
were King Wén's plans!
How great the inheritance
of King Wǔ's achievements!
They enlighten and assist us, their descendants,
all to be correct without deficiency.'
You must reverently clarify your instructions,
to serve and follow the former kings.
'Respond to and display the glorious mandate of Wén and Wǔ,'
to match the former men.
The king spoke thus:
"Jūn Yá!
You should follow the former ministers' old statutes as your model,
for the people's order or disorder lies herein.
Follow the conduct of your grandfather and father,
and illuminate your sovereign's governance."
King Mù commanded Bó Jiǒng
to become the Grand Coachman of Zhōu.
The "Jiǒng Mìng" was composed.
The king spoke thus:
"Bó Jiǒng!
I am unable in virtue,
yet succeed my ancestors as the great sovereign.
Apprehensive and cautious, I am ever vigilant,
rising in the middle of the night,
thinking how to avoid errors.
In the past, under Wén and Wǔ, they were intelligent, wise, and sagely.
Ministers great and small
all cherished loyalty and goodness.
Their attendants, guards, and followers
were none but upright men.
Morning and evening they assisted their sovereign,
in going out and coming in, rising and resting,
there was nothing not respected.
Issuing commands and decrees,
there was nothing not good.
The lower people reverently complied,
and all states enjoyed tranquility.
'I alone am without goodness,'
truly relying on the officers left and right, before and behind,
to correct my shortcomings,
rectify errors and correct mistakes,
straighten my wrongful thoughts,
enabling me to continue the illustrious achievements.
Now I appoint you as Grand Coachman,
to oversee the multitude of attendants and serving ministers.
Encourage your sovereign's virtue,
and mutually correct what is lacking.
Carefully select your colleagues,
not allowing those with clever words and ingratiating looks,
flatterers and sycophants,
but only good men.
If the servant ministers are upright,
their sovereign can be upright;
if the servant ministers are flattering,
their sovereign will consider himself sage.
The sovereign's virtue depends on the ministers,
his lack of virtue also depends on the ministers.
Do not be intimate with petty men,
filling the offices of ears and eyes,
leading the superior against the statutes of the former kings.
If not men are considered good,
but only goods are considered good,
thus, 'they neglect their offices,'
then you greatly fail to reverence your sovereign,
and I will hold you guilty."
The king said:
"Alas!
Be reverent!
Forever assist your sovereign with constant laws."
Lǚ gave commands, King Mù instructed on the Xìa system of redemption punishments.
The "Lǚ Xíng" was composed.
It was Lǚ who gave commands.
The king, having reigned for a hundred years,
aged and vast, considered making punishments
to restrain the four quarters.
The king said:
"According to ancient teachings,
Chīyóu first created disorder,
which spread to the common people.
None were not robbers and thieves,
owl-like in righteousness, treacherous and rebellious,
seizing, plundering, and falsely claiming.
The Miáo people did not follow the spirits,
so they controlled them with punishments;
they made the five oppressive punishments,
calling them laws.
They slaughtered the innocent.
Then they began to excessively practice cutting off noses, feet, castration, and tattooing;
thus, applying punishments and creating laws,
showing no difference to those with pleas.
The people arose and gradually deteriorated,
in chaos and confusion;
there was no sincerity in good faith,
so they broke their oaths and covenants.
The oppressive rulers and the multitude of afflicted
reported their innocence to Heaven.
The Lord on High surveyed the people,
there were no fragrant virtues,
only the stench of punishments was heard.
The August Emperor pitied the multitude of afflicted innocents,
repressing oppression with majesty,
exterminating the Miáo people,
so they had no descendants below.
Then he commanded Zhòng and Lí
